summary: Describes how to store the parameters needed to validate a private key inside the PKCS#8 private-key format of RFC 5208, and also the alternative format in RFC 5958.

eli5.summary: A secret key comes with notes so you can check it is not broken. This says where to tuck the notes in.

questions: how do you validate rsa key parameters
how to store key validation data
subtitle: Attaching validation proofs to stored RSA and DSA private keys.

tldr.problem: RSA and DSA private keys generated with the Shawe-Taylor algorithm can be validated to check that primes are genuine, but the standard PKCS#8 private-key format has no way to store the validation parameters.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a private-key attribute in PKCS#8 that holds a hash algorithm identifier and a seed value, allowing validation of the key's primes.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can now verify the integrity of generated private keys without needing external validation data, though this method does not form part of a formal standard.

today: RFC 8479 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It provides a de facto method for storing validation parameters with private keys, though the method remains optional and is not part of a formal standard.

sections.title: Validating Private Keys
sections.content:
Private keys in cryptography, especially RSA and DSA keys, rely on the mathematical properties of prime numbers. Keys generated using the Shawe-Taylor prime generation algorithm from FIPS 186-4 can be validated by re-generating the primes from a known seed and comparing them to the key material. This validation confirms that the primes are genuinely prime and were correctly generated.

The PKCS#8 format (RFC 5208) and its successor, Asymmetric Key Packages (RFC 5958), define how to store private key material. However, these formats do not include a standard way to store the seed and hash algorithm needed to perform this validation. This document defines such a method.
sections.eli5: When you create a secret key from prime numbers, you can prove the primes are real by checking them the same way you made them. This explains how to save that proof inside the key file.

sections.title: ValidationParams Attribute
sections.content:
The validation parameters are stored as an attribute in the PrivateKeyInfo structure using the object identifier id-attr-validation-parameters with the value {1 3 6 1 4 1 2312 18 8 1}. This is a private enterprise extension and does not form part of a formal standard.

The ValidationParams structure is a sequence containing two fields: hashAlgo, which is an object identifier for the hash algorithm used during key generation, and seed, which is an octet string containing the original seed. The sequence must be DER encoded according to ITU-T Recommendation X.690.
sections.eli5: The validation data is stored in two parts: which hash method was used, and the random starting number that made the primes.

sections.title: Example Structure
sections.content: The document provides a concrete example of an RSA key generated using the algorithm from Section B.3.3 of FIPS 186-4 with SHA2-384 as the hash algorithm. The seed used in this example is 8af4328c87bebcec31e303b8f5537effcb6a91d947084d99a369823b36f01462 (in hexadecimal). The example shows how the complete private key structure, including the validation parameters attribute, is encoded in base64 format in a PEM container.
sections.eli5: Here is a real example: an actual secret key with its validation proof stored inside, showing exactly what it looks like.

sections.title: Compatibility and Applicability
sections.content:
For compatibility with existing implementations, this document recommends that any implementation supporting this extension should handle validation using the SHA2-384 hash algorithm. The extension applies equally to both PKCS#8 (RFC 5208) and Asymmetric Key Packages (RFC 5958), making it useful across different private-key management systems.

The approach described does not require formal standardization; implementations can adopt this method directly as is, or use it as a foundation for a standard at a later time. The security considerations of both RFC 5208 and RFC 5958 apply fully to this extension.
sections.eli5: Different key systems can use this same way of storing validation data, and if they support SHA2-384 hashing, they will work well together.
